definition.text: The plant organ, usually below the soil surface, that anchors the plant and takes in water and dissolved nutrients.

facts.text: Roots anchor the plant, absorb water and dissolved minerals and conduct them to the shoot; they also store reserves, make growth regulators and support symbiotic nutrient uptake.
Root epidermal cells and root hairs take up soil water and dissolved ions, which then move to the shoot through the xylem.
A root system's depth and spread decide which soil horizons the plant can draw water and nutrients from.
The root cap helps a new root push through soil; its cells are sloughed off as the root deepens, leaving a slimy, lubricating surface.
The roots of most vascular plants form mycorrhizae with certain fungi, and many other organisms, bacteria among them, live closely with roots.
Grass roots hold soil together and reduce erosion, and the decay of old roots of perennial rangeland grasses adds organic matter and releases nutrients.
Fossil roots, mostly infilled voids left where roots rotted, go back to the late Silurian, about 430 million years ago, and are easily confused with animal burrows.

events.date_text: late Silurian, about 430 million years ago

definition.text: The spatial layout of a plant's whole root system: how its roots branch, spread and angle through the soil.

facts.text: Architecture depends on the plant species, the soil's composition and the nutrients available, and it secures water, nutrients and anchorage.
It is described by branching pattern (herringbone, dichotomous or radial), link length between branches, link radius and root angle.
Outside influences include gravity, light, water and oxygen, and the supply or lack of nitrogen, phosphorus, sulphur, aluminium and sodium chloride.
A root system that developed in dry soil may work less well when the soil floods.

definition.text: How a plant's roots are spread down through the soil, which depends on the plant's form, where and when water and nutrients are available, and the soil's physical properties.

facts.text: Most roots of most plants lie fairly close to the surface, where nutrients are more available and aeration is better.
Rock, compacted soil close below the surface or anaerobic conditions can physically limit rooting depth.
The deepest roots are generally found in deserts and temperate coniferous forests, the shallowest in tundra, boreal forest and temperate grasslands.
In continuous permafrost, roots cannot go below the active layer, so plants must be shallow-rooted and trees are limited to specialists such as larch.
Some roots grow as deep as the tree is tall; the deepest living root observed, at least 60 metres (200 ft) down, turned up in an open-pit mine in Arizona.

conflicts.text: The page's records table gives a maximum rooting depth of 68 m for Boscia albitrunca in the Kalahari desert.
conflicts.note: Deeper than the 'at least 60 metres' given for the deepest observed living root on the same page; the table may include roots not confirmed living.

definition.text: The ways roots sense their surroundings, such as gravity, light, physical barriers and soil conditions, and steer their growth in response.

facts.text: Gravitropism, worked through auxin pathways, sends roots downward from germination, and different root types hold different set angles of growth.
Air, mineral nutrients and water steer root growth, and roots turn away from dry or otherwise poor soil.
Roots searching for nutrients can sense and avoid compacted soil through the diffusion of the gas ethylene.
Roots can tell their own roots from other plants' roots in the same soil, and over time they can crack foundations, snap water lines and lift sidewalks.

title: Specialized root types

definition.text: Root forms adapted to tasks beyond anchorage and uptake, such as aerial, prop, buttress, storage, contractile and cluster roots.

facts.text: Cluster or proteoid roots are dense clusters of rootlets of limited growth that form under low phosphate or low iron, notably in the Proteaceae.
Aerating roots, or pneumatophores, rise above ground or water so that mangroves and other plants can exchange gases where soil oxygen is limited.
Root nodules, found in virtually all legumes, house nitrogen-fixing soil bacteria; coralloid roots near the soil surface house nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.
Contractile roots pull bulbs, corms and some taproots deeper into the soil by expanding radially and contracting lengthwise.

notes: The section's opening sentence (S:ef31ea790b52) carries a CLARIFICATION NEEDED tag.

title: Fibrous root system

definition.text: A root system of many thin, similar-sized roots growing from the stem base and forming a dense mat near the soil surface, the opposite of a taproot system.

facts.text: It is universal in monocots and ferns, with grasses such as wheat and rice as typical examples; in many species the network is mostly adventitious roots from the stem base.
It arises when the embryonic root dies back while the plant is young, leaving a mass of fine roots with no distinct taproot.
Fibrous roots bind soil, take up surface nutrients quickly and control erosion; forage crops cover the whole field and anchor its top layer of soil.
Most trees switch from a taproot to a wide fibrous system within a few years; a mature tree 30–50 m tall spreads roots as far as its height or more, with well over 95% in the top 50 cm.
Root mats of meadow grasses may help immobilise radioactive materials in soil.

notes: Taproot (S:8ba9b5da5989) says as much as 100% of a mature tree's roots lie in the top 50 cm, against 'well over 95%' here; compatible bounds, not entered as a conflict.

image.caption: Kumar83, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

definition.text: A large, central, dominant root, usually straight, thick and tapering, from which smaller roots branch sideways.

facts.text: Dicots start with a taproot grown from the seed's radicle; it may last the plant's life but is more often replaced by a fibrous root system.
Soil shapes taproots: deep, rich soils favour vertical taproots in many oaks, while clay soils promote several taproots.
Many taproots are storage organs, as in carrot, radish and turnip.
Taprooted plants are hard to transplant, and deep-rooted weeds such as dandelion resprout unless the taproot is cut several centimetres below ground.

definition.text: A thin outgrowth of a single epidermal cell near the root tip that collects water and mineral nutrients from the soil.

facts.text: Root hairs raise the root's surface area relative to its volume, and most of a root's water uptake passes through them.
They are 15–17 micrometres across and 80–1,500 micrometres long, and their length lets them reach in between soil particles.
They grow only in the zone of maturation, perhaps because older hairs are sheared off as the root elongates through the soil.
Root hair cells secrete malic and citric acids, which solubilise minerals by changing their oxidation state so that the ions are easier to absorb.
They are the main interface with mycorrhizal fungi; ectomycorrhizal fungi colonise root hairs first, then build a Hartig net in the outer root cortex.
In legumes, root hairs curl around rhizobia so that an infection thread can grow into dividing cortical cells and form a nodule.
Transplanting or repotting can strip off many root hairs and make the plant wilt.

image.caption: Unknown author, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

title: Root mucilage

definition.text: A gelatinous secretion of plant-specific polysaccharides, part of the root exudate, that coats the root cap.

facts.text: It seems to come from root-cap cells that are continually shed and burst as roots push through soil, releasing polysaccharides made in the Golgi apparatus and cell walls.
Maize mucilage is rich in galactose, xylose, arabinose, rhamnose and glucose; these sugars build plant polysaccharides such as pectin, xyloglucan, arabinan and xylan.
Plants use up to 40% of their energy, made by photosynthesis in the leaves, secreting root mucilage.
Mucilage makes soil stick to roots, keeping the contact needed to regulate water uptake, cutting friction as roots penetrate and maintaining a microclimate.
It shapes the hydrophysical properties of the rhizosphere: it can reduce evaporation and store water, which affects how plants cope with water deficit.
It helps build symbioses with soil fungi, which feed on broken-down mucilage and in return raise the plant's uptake of water and nutrients, particularly phosphorus.
The aerial roots of Sierra Mixe maize secrete a sweet mucilage whose high-sugar, low-oxygen conditions support nitrogen-fixing bacteria, letting it grow on poor soils without fertiliser.

contested_note: The source calls the way mucilage is secreted debated, though growing evidence points to ruptured root-cap cells.

title: Root exudates

definition.text: The organic compounds, such as sugars, amino acids, proteins, enzymes and DNA, that plant roots release into the surrounding soil.

facts.text: Exudates help protect roots against bacterial and fungal infection, help them penetrate the soil and can create a microclimate that benefits the plant.
Root exudation supports microbial activity, and exudates are a source of soil carbon.
Exudates such as organic acids change the chemistry and biological communities of the rhizosphere relative to the bulk soil.
Different plant species release different exudates and so recruit different microbial communities from the bulk soil into their rhizosphere.
Root and microbial exudates can extract phosphorus from apatite, the most common mineral source of soil phosphorus.
Exudates called strigolactones, together with soil phosphorus, control how arbuscular mycorrhizal hyphae grow through the soil.
Roughly 5% of a plant's photosynthetically fixed carbon is estimated to pass into soil as root exudates, though it is hard to quantify.
Arabidopsis seedlings grow more lateral roots in exudates of non-kin than of kin, which may let plants spend less on competition among relatives.

notes: No 'Plant root exudates' article was crawled; passes the two-or-more-pages test (Root mucilage, Rhizosphere, Soil formation, Soil carbon, Disease suppressive soils, Arbuscular mycorrhiza, Plant nutrients in soil).

definition.text: The narrow zone of soil directly influenced by root secretions and by the microorganisms that live with the roots.

facts.text: The German plant physiologist Lorenz Hiltner coined the term in 1904 for a zone around roots whose microbes are partly controlled by chemicals the roots release.
Microbes in its pores feed on sloughed-off root cells (rhizodeposition) and on the proteins and sugars that roots release (root exudates).
Up to 10 billion culturable bacterial cells inhabit each gram of soil in and around roots, making the rhizosphere a hotspot of microbial diversity.
Roots may exude 20–40% of their photosynthetically fixed carbon as sugars and organic acids.
Much of the nutrient cycling plants need, and disease suppression by antibiotics, happens right beside roots because of exudates and microbial products.
Organic acids and sugars there affect how microbes shuttle phosphorus, nitrogen, potassium and water to the root, and how much iron is available.
Root respiration and exudation can create anoxic microsites next to roots, and in acid soils the pH is raised close to roots.
The rhizoplane is the root surface itself together with the soil particles closely bound to it.

definition.text: The web of mutualism, predation and competition among the microbes and soil animals that rhizodeposition supports around and inside roots.

facts.text: Its food web has three channels with two energy sources: fungal and bacterial channels run on detritus, while nematodes, symbionts and some arthropods run on root energy.
The bacterial channel turns over faster than the fungal one, because bacteria use more accessible resources and regenerate faster.
Predation by bacteria-feeding nematodes has been shown to affect nitrogen availability and plant growth.
Plants and soil microbes compete indirectly by locking limiting carbon and nitrogen into their biomass, and plants take up organic nitrogen such as amino acids less well than rhizosphere microbes.
Groups of interacting microbes, such as growth-promoting bacteria with mycorrhizal fungi or Trichoderma, can give plants additive or synergistic benefits.
Long-term monoculture can override the natural selection of microbes and cause 'soil sickness', a shift in pathogenic and beneficial populations that lowers soil fertility and yield.
Exudates that build up over time can harm the host: in aged tea plantations, soil polyphenols have been linked to a harmful microbial shift and soil sickness.

definition.text: The exchange of chemical signals among roots, microbes, fungi and insects in the rhizosphere, which shapes which organisms colonise the root zone.

facts.text: Hundreds of metabolites released by roots mainly shape and recruit the rhizosphere's microbial community, letting plants favour growth-promoting rhizobacteria.
Rhizobia detect flavonoids from legume roots and answer with nod factors that lead to root nodules; these signals are strictly specific to plant and bacterium.
Strigolactones from roots make mycorrhizal spores germinate and colonise the root, but the parasitic plant Striga also germinates when it detects them.
Nutrients released by plants also attract pathogens, which use plant products to survive in the rhizosphere.

title: Allelopathy

definition.text: The release by some plants, often from their roots, of chemicals that hold back the growth of other organisms.

facts.text: Invasive garlic mustard is believed to stop trees forming mycorrhizae in North American forests; its allelochemical benzyl isothiocyanate inhibited three ectomycorrhizal fungi on white pine seedlings.
Some cover crops suppress weeds through allelopathy, among them rye, hairy vetch, red clover, sorghum-sudangrass and mustards.
Crop rotation relieves allelopathy as well as raising yields through better nutrient availability.

notes: No Allelopathy article crawled; passes the two-or-more-pages test (Rhizosphere, Ectomycorrhiza, Cover crop, Crop rotation).

definition.text: Field and laboratory techniques for studying the root zone, from pH measurements to DNA sequencing of its microbes.

facts.text: Marker genes, 16S rRNA for bacteria and the ITS region for fungi, are amplified and sequenced to find a community's composition and diversity.
Metagenomics and metatranscriptomics sequence all the DNA or RNA present to assess a community's genetic potential and active gene expression.
Microelectrodes, agar techniques and microsampling follow pH and water movement in the rhizosphere.
Pyrolysis–field ionization mass spectrometry detects fulvic and humic acids and humins in field soils.

title: Rhizodeposition

definition.text: The addition of organic matter to soil by living roots, which exude compounds and slough off cells, especially at their tips.

facts.text: Rhizodeposits supply many forms of organic carbon and nitrogen that feed the communities around roots and strongly change the chemistry next to them.
They stimulate bacterial activity in the rhizosphere, whereas most bacteria in the bulk soil stay quiescent.
Together with fungal hyphae and microbial extracellular polymers, rhizodeposition enmeshes soil and improves aggregate stability.

notes: No article of its own; passes the two-or-more-pages test (Rhizosphere, Soil formation, Soil microbiology, Tilth).

definition.text: The soil outside the rhizosphere, not penetrated by plant roots.

facts.text: Natural organic compounds are much scarcer in bulk soil than in the rhizosphere.
Microbes are more varied in bulk soil but more abundant in the rhizosphere, and bulk-soil organisms are generally smaller than the same species near roots.
Bulk soil tends to have smaller pores and more moisture at a given matric potential than the rhizosphere, which affects which microbes survive there.
Away from roots most bacteria are quiescent, in mucilaginous colonies glued with clay particles that protect them from drying out and from protozoa and nematodes.
Its chemical properties include organic matter, organic carbon, nutrient content, cation-exchange capacity, free ions, pH and base saturation.
Bulk-soil respiration responds to temperature swings, and added nutrients or warming can strongly change its microbes, especially in sandy soils.

definition.text: The zone around a germinating seed where soil, microorganisms and the seed interact.

facts.text: It typically reaches 1–10 mm from the seed, varying with seed type, the soil's microbes, soil moisture and other factors.
Seed exudates inhibit or stimulate microbes, but soil type, especially its organic matter content, matters much more than seed type.
Pathogens such as Fusarium and Pythium ultimum can colonise a seed within hours of planting, but seeds can attract beneficial microbes that keep them out.
Short-lived as it is, the spermosphere grows into the rhizosphere below once the radicle emerges, and into the laimosphere and phyllosphere above.

definition.text: The changing community of microorganisms, mainly bacteria, fungi and archaea, that lives with plant roots.

facts.text: The communities inside the root, in the rhizosphere and in bulk soil differ from one another, though some species overlap.
Beneficial members include nitrogen-fixing bacteria, growth-promoting microbes, mycorrhizal fungi, protozoa and biocontrol organisms; harmful ones include some bacteria, fungi and nematodes.
Root symbionts live on carbon-rich products of the host plant's photosynthesis.
Mycorrhizal fungi extend far into the bulk soil, widening the root system's reach and surface area.
Microbes cover only part of the root surface, about 10% of three-week-old root segments and about 37% of three-month-old roots, though before the 1970s most was thought covered.
Methanogens and ammonia-oxidizing archaea are common root microbes, especially in anaerobic soils and wetlands.
Plants recruit selectively: in finger millet only about 8% of the core microbiota was consistently shared between soil and plant.

definition.text: The idea that a root microbe can behave anywhere from mutualist to parasite, depending on its host, the environment and the host's health.

facts.text: Parasites take carbon from the plant while giving no benefit, or too little for what they take, and so lower the host's fitness.
The host's immune response controls symbiont infection and growth; if it fails, the relationship slides toward the parasitic end.
High nutrient levels can push some microbes into parasitic behaviour at a time when the plant no longer needs their help to get nutrients.
Symbionts may be biotrophic, living off living tissue, or necrotrophic, living off dead tissue.

title: Root microbiome assembly

definition.text: How individual microbes come together into the communities found on and around roots, a question with two competing explanations.

facts.text: One hypothesis holds that 'everything is everywhere, but the environment selects'; the other that neutral processes such as distance and dispersal barriers decide when taxa are equally fit.
Most likely both selection and neutral processes act, with some taxa more limited by one than the other.
Root tips, fine roots, the root surface and the rhizosphere each host different communities, as exudates supply carbon compounds that select microbes with matching metabolism.
Nutrient levels, pH, moisture, temperature, soil structure and disturbance also shape assembly, because microbes differ in their optima.

contested_note: The source describes an ongoing debate between environmental selection and neutral dispersal as the drivers of root microbial community assembly.

definition.text: Bacteria that live with plant roots and can harm, have no effect on, or benefit plant growth.

facts.text: The term usually means bacteria in mutualism with plants, often called plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR); about 2–5% of rhizosphere bacteria are PGPR.
Some colonise the root surface or the spaces between outer root cells, often forming nodules; others live as endophytes inside the plant's apoplast.
One of their most useful acts is nitrogen fixation, turning N2 gas, which plants cannot use, into ammonia the host can take up.
Building and keeping root nodules for rhizobacteria can cost a plant 12–25% of its total photosynthetic output.
Organic acids and phosphatases released by rhizobacteria turn insoluble soil phosphorus into plant-available forms such as H2PO4−.
Free-living nitrogen fixers also live just outside the roots of many grasses; in rice they supply more fixed nitrogen when the plant's demand is high.
Organic amendments such as sugarcane straw, goat manure and filter mud boost free-living growth-promoting bacteria, improving nitrogen fixation and phosphorus solubilisation even without nodules.
Legumes enrich the soil around them through their bacteria, which is why they have long been used in crop rotation, though it can also sharpen competition with other plants.

definition.text: Soil bacteria that colonise plant roots, after being inoculated onto seed, and enhance plant growth.

facts.text: Joseph W. Kloepper first used the term PGPR in the late 1970s.
Direct mechanisms include fixing nitrogen, making siderophores that chelate iron for the root, solubilising minerals such as phosphorus and making plant hormones.
Indirectly they limit the damage pathogens do to yield, suppressing disease through induced systemic resistance and antifungal metabolites.
To work they must survive on the seed, multiply in the spermosphere, attach to the root and colonise the root system; failure to colonise often explains poor field results.
Inoculants are often applied to the seed coat, so that a large enough population establishes in the rhizosphere; bacteria at the root tip were found to be most active.
Most are Pseudomonadota and Bacillota, with many Pseudomonas and Bacillus; Pseudomonas putida and Azospirillum lipoferum are examples.
Developing PGPR into biofertilisers and biopesticides could raise yields and cut disease while reducing dependence on chemical fertilisers and pesticides.

definition.text: Root-colonising bacteria that harm plant growth, first described from sugar beet crops.

facts.text: Sugar beet seeds inoculated with them germinated less and had root lesions, short and distorted roots, more fungal infection and poorer growth; one trial lost 48% of yield.
Six strains have been identified, in the genera Enterobacter, Klebsiella, Citrobacter, Flavobacterium, Achromobacter and Arthrobacter.
Growth-promoting rhizobacteria hold them back: plots given both rose 39% in production, while plots given only deleterious strains fell 30%.

definition.text: A symbiosis between a fungus and a plant in which fungal hyphae and plant roots interconnect and form an interface at the level of cells.

facts.text: The plant gives the fungus sugars or lipids made by photosynthesis; the fungus gives the plant water and soil nutrients such as phosphorus, nitrogen and zinc.
The fungus colonises root tissue either inside the cells, as in arbuscular mycorrhizas, or between them, as in ectomycorrhizas.
The association is normally mutualistic, but in some species or circumstances it can be parasitic.
Mycorrhizas occur in 92% of plant families studied (80% of species), but some families, such as Brassicaceae and Chenopodiaceae, cannot form them.
In some ecosystems up to 80% of plant nitrogen and 90% of plant phosphorus comes through mycorrhizal fungi, and plants may give them about 20–40% of their carbon.
The plant's need for phosphorus is a strong trigger: arbuscular fungi are recruited when the plant senses phosphorus starvation, and nitrogen starvation also plays a part.
Mycorrhizae emerged as early as 450–500 million years ago, and proto-mycorrhizal fungi may have been key to plants colonising land.

verification.evidence: Of particular importance for forestry and agricultural systems is the cooperative and mutualistic interaction between plant roots and arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi from the phylum Glomeromycotina, since about 80% of terrestrial plant species can form AM symbiosis.

image.caption: Unknown author, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

definition.text: The trade in which a mycorrhizal fungus gets carbohydrates from its host and in return improves the plant's uptake of water and minerals.

facts.text: Sugars such as glucose and sucrose move from their source, usually the leaves, to the roots and on to the fungus.
Most mycorrhizal hyphae are far finer than the smallest root or root hair, so they explore soil that roots cannot reach and add absorbing surface.
Fungi may secrete organic acids that dissolve or chelate ions, or release ions from minerals by ion exchange.
Hyphae reach phosphate and iron that roots alone cannot, including nutrients immobilised in clay-rich or strongly basic soils.
Some mycorrhizal fungi decay organic matter directly; in some nutrient-poor forests their hyphae take phosphate straight from leaf litter, bypassing soil uptake.
Inga alley cropping, proposed as an alternative to slash-and-burn, relies on mycorrhizae in Inga roots to stop rain washing phosphorus out of the soil.
Mycorrhizae help most in nutrient-poor soils, but in boreal forests fungi have been found hoarding nitrogen in times of scarcity, so the trade may be more than simply mutualistic.

title: Mycorrhizal types

definition.text: The grouping of mycorrhizas by how the fungus colonises the root, with the main split between ectomycorrhizas and endomycorrhizas.

facts.text: Ectomycorrhizal hyphae do not enter individual root cells, whereas endomycorrhizal hyphae pass through the cell wall up to the cell membrane.
Arbuscular, ericoid, arbutoid, monotropoid and orchid mycorrhizas all count as endomycorrhizae.
The mycorrhizal lifestyle evolved independently many times: arbuscular fungi form a single phylum, while other mycorrhizal fungi converged on similar ways of life.
Fungal endophytes live harmlessly inside plants but lack the structures mycorrhizal fungi use to bring in nutrients from outside the plant.
Mucoromycotina 'fine root endophytes' were long mistaken for arbuscular fungi; they seem able to live without a host and prefer wet, acidic soils.
In monotropoid mycorrhizas, found in Monotropoideae and some orchids, the plant takes its carbon from the fungus, making the association parasitic.

notes: The monotropoid 'parasitic' sentence (S:bdba3d5ea7c3) carries a CITATION NEEDED tag.

image.caption: Malene Thyssen, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

definition.text: The ability of a few plant species to host both arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal fungi in the same root system at once.

facts.text: Its costs and benefits seem to depend on the plant's life stage and abiotic conditions, and switching between fungal types has also been reported.
Dual-mycorrhizal plants often have broader ranges, spreading into habitats where one of the fungal types is missing.
They aid succession and ecosystem recovery on nutrient-poor soils and are valued in restoration where trees lack fungal inoculum.
Ectomycorrhizal woodland trees have been seen establishing around dual-mycorrhizal willows within vegetation dominated by arbuscular mycorrhizas.

title: Mycorrhizal stress protection
article: Mycorrhiza#Disease, drought and salinity resistance and its correlation to mycorrhizae

definition.text: The protection mycorrhizal fungi give plants against soil-borne disease, drought, salt and toxic metals.

facts.text: Mycorrhizal plants are often more resistant to soil-borne pathogens, and mycorrhizas secrete enzymes toxic to soil organisms such as nematodes.
Forming the association primes the plant's immune system, so its defence responses are stronger.
Mycorrhizal fungi were correlated with soil water level, not aggregate stability, and can make plants more resistant to drought.
Salinity can harm the fungi, yet many reports show mycorrhizal plants growing better under salt stress.
Fungi protect plants rooted in acidic, contaminated or metal-rich soils; pines inoculated with Pisolithus tinctorius tolerated contaminated sites well.
Zinc-tolerant Suillus bovinus protected Scots pine, probably by binding the metal in its external mycelium without blocking useful exchange.

definition.text: The part mycorrhizal fungi play in helping plants establish on sterile, barren or degraded soils.

facts.text: Plants in sterile soils and growth media often do poorly unless spores or hyphae of mycorrhizal fungi are added to colonise their roots.
Without mycorrhizal fungi, plant growth can lag in early succession and on degraded land.
Introducing alien mycorrhizal plants into nutrient-poor ecosystems puts native non-mycorrhizal plants at a disadvantage.
Tuberculate ectomycorrhizae of Suillus tomentosus on lodgepole pine host nitrogen-fixing bacteria, which let the pines colonise nutrient-poor sites.

definition.text: How rising carbon dioxide, warming and air pollution affect mycorrhizal fungi and the plants that rely on them.

facts.text: More carbon dioxide should directly benefit plants and mycorrhizae if nothing else is limiting, but climate change may also damage mycorrhizae.
Mycorrhizae tend to do better in cool conditions, so warming could harm them; in the Arctic, where nitrogen and water are hard to get, they are crucial to plant growth.
SO2, NOx and ozone from human activity may reduce propagules, root colonisation, links between trees and ectomycorrhizal enzyme activity.
Air pollution, including the breakdown of excess atmospheric ammonia, can damage fine mycorrhizal structures.

title: Common mycorrhizal network

definition.text: An underground network formed where the hyphae of mycorrhizal fungi join the roots of two or more plants, of the same or different species, linking them together.

facts.text: The two main types follow the fungi: arbuscular networks, whose hyphae enter root cells, and ectomycorrhizal networks, whose hyphae thread between cells; northern temperate and boreal canopy trees tend to be ectomycorrhizal.
Partnerships are usually mutualistic but can be commensal or parasitic and can switch over time; network formation depends on soil fertility, resources, genotypes, disturbance and season.

Studies report carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus moving between plants through arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal networks, with nitrogen flowing from nitrogen-fixing to non-fixing plants along a source–sink gradient.
Carbon-isotope labelling showed carbon moving both ways between paper birch and Douglas fir, its direction shifting with the seasons; the fir ended with a 2% to 3% net gain.

Reported benefits include better seedling establishment, growth and survival, and transfer of water, carbon and nitrogen that helps plants colonize less favourable sites; not all plants are compatible with all networks.
Linked plants are reported to pass on warnings: an insect-damaged Douglas fir appeared to signal a nearby ponderosa pine, which then made defence enzymes.
Suzanne Simard described the networks in 1997; their apparent roles in woodland earned them the nickname 'Wood Wide Web'.

Claims that networks are ubiquitous, move resources between plants and carry warnings are criticised as weakly supported; connections are hard to verify in the field, and transfer may pass through the soil instead.

contested_note: Mycorrhizal network says claims of resource transfer and warning signals through networks are not strongly supported, and Mycorrhiza says the birch-to-fir carbon transfer was not shown to pass through a network, against reports of network-mediated transfer.
notes: Extended in gap-fill with the crawled Mycorrhizal network page. Also on Mycorrhiza, Ectomycorrhiza, Soil biology, Arbuscular mycorrhiza.

verification.evidence: Mycorrhizal networks promoted seedling growth in 48% of the cases (for 21 seedling species), while negative effects (25%) and no effects (27%) were also common.
verification.note: the paper gives the share of studies where networks helped seedlings (48%); the entry gives the fir's net carbon gain (2-3%)

definition.text: The study of root–fungus partnerships from nineteenth-century observations to genome sequencing.

facts.text: In 1881 Franciszek Kamieński showed that Monotropa hypopitys depends on fungi from neighbouring trees for nutrition; A.B. Frank formally described and named mycorrhizal fungi in 1885.
In 1899 Noël Bernard established that orchids such as Neottia nidus-avis need a specific fungus to germinate.
Paleobotanists working on the Rhynie chert showed that mycorrhiza-like associations existed in early land plants 407 million years ago.
In 2008 Laccaria bicolor became the first ectomycorrhizal fungus to have its genome sequenced, opening the molecular era of mycorrhizal research.

title: Arbuscular mycorrhiza

definition.text: A type of mycorrhiza in which the fungus enters the cortical cells of a plant's roots and forms tree-like arbuscules inside them.

facts.text: Arbuscules are the sites where phosphorus, carbon, water and other nutrients are exchanged; balloon-like vesicles often store reserves.
It is formed by fungi of the Glomeromycotina and some Mucoromycotina, and helps plants capture phosphorus, sulphur, nitrogen and micronutrients from the soil.
It is the most widespread plant symbiosis known, found in 80% of vascular plant families and about 80% of plant species, on every continent except Antarctica.
The fungi are obligate symbionts with little ability to live on dead matter, and up to 20% of the host plant's carbon may pass to them.
Earth's topsoils hold an estimated 110 quadrillion kilometres of arbuscular fungal hyphae, about 40% of it in wild grasslands, with a biomass of about 300 megatons of carbon.
These fungi are most frequent on mineral soils and vital on nutrient-poor volcanic soils and sand dunes, but colonisation is lower in very arid or nutrient-rich soils.
Their extraradical hyphae and the soil protein glomalin improve soil aggregate stability.
Members of the mustard family, such as cabbage, cauliflower and canola, do not form arbuscular mycorrhizas.

title: Arbuscular mycorrhizal nutrient exchange

definition.text: The trade in which arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi take sugars from their host and supply it above all with phosphorus.

facts.text: The fungi take up the host's photosynthetic products as hexoses and store carbon as trehalose, glycogen and lipids; about 25% of the carbon they receive is stored in their extraradical hyphae.
Phosphorus reaches roots mainly by diffusion; hyphae shorten the distance, and phosphorus can flow into mycorrhizae up to six times faster than into root hairs.
In some cases the hyphal network takes over phosphorus uptake entirely, and all of a plant's phosphorus may come through the fungus.
More carbon to the fungus means more phosphorus back to the plant, and less means less; some fungi are poor partners that take much carbon for little phosphorus.
Mycorrhizae lower root-zone pH by taking up ammonium selectively and releasing H+ ions, which makes phosphorus precipitates more soluble.
Hyphal uptake of ammonium also increases the flow of nitrogen to the plant.
As their hyphal network grows and dies back, the fungi add a substantial amount of carbon to the rhizosphere and to the below-ground organic carbon pool.

title: Arbuscular mycorrhizae in agriculture

definition.text: Managing tillage, fertiliser and cropping so that crops can form working partnerships with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.

facts.text: Tillage, heavy fertiliser and fungicide use, poor rotations and breeding for such conditions all hinder crops' symbiosis with arbuscular fungi.
Tillage breaks up soil macrostructure and the hyphal network, leaving it non-infective and cutting phosphorus supply; reduced-tillage systems may need less phosphorus fertiliser.
Heavy phosphorus fertiliser inhibits colonisation; as plant phosphorus rises the fungal carbon drain stops paying, and lost colonisation can cause deficiencies of micronutrients such as copper.
Cover crops extend fungal growth through autumn, winter and spring, and the extraradical mycelium survives winter to colonise the next crop early.
Crops poor at finding nutrients, such as flax, depend heavily on arbuscular fungi for phosphorus at low and intermediate soil phosphorus levels.
Managing the fungi matters most in organic and low-input systems, where soil phosphorus is generally low and their benefits are greatest.

distinct_from: Arbuscular mycorrhizal effects on soil communities

title: Mycorrhizal inoculation for land restoration

definition.text: Adding arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi to soil when replanting degraded land, to rebuild its biological and physical properties.

facts.text: Disturbing native plant cover in areas threatened by desertification often degrades soil structure, nutrient availability and organic matter.
A mixture of native arbuscular fungi improved soil quality over the long term more than a single exotic species or no inoculum.
Benefits included more plant growth, phosphorus uptake, soil nitrogen and organic matter, and better aggregation, infiltration and aeration, helped by more legume nodulation.
Restoring native fungi speeds soil recovery, and native strains help extract heavy metals from polluted soils.

distinct_from: Arbuscular mycorrhizal effects on soil communities

title: Arbuscular mycorrhizal effects on soil communities

definition.text: The ways arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis shapes the bacteria, plants and other organisms living in the soil around roots.

facts.text: By changing the amount and makeup of root and fungal exudates, colonisation decides the diversity and abundance of rhizosphere bacteria.
Rhizobia in the soil raise mycorrhizal colonisation, and good colonisation in turn increases nodulation and nitrogen fixation in legumes.
Greater mycorrhizal diversity increases plant diversity, and dominant arbuscular fungi can keep non-mycorrhizal plants from invading.
Arbuscular fungi become less common and less diverse at higher soil nutrient and moisture levels, as plants give them less carbon.

title: Detecting arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi
article: Arbuscular mycorrhiza#Molecular genetic analyses of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi

definition.text: Molecular and chemical techniques for finding and measuring arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi in roots and soil.

facts.text: DNA analyses use markers in the nuclear ribosomal operon (18S rRNA), and quantitative PCR measures targeted fungal DNA in roots or soil.
The phospholipid fatty acid 16:1ω5 is the most used marker of fungal mycelial biomass in soil; with 18:1ω7 it makes up about 58% of their phospholipid fatty acids.
Neutral lipids store energy in spores and vesicles, so the ratio of neutral-lipid to phospholipid 16:1ω5 shows how much carbon goes to storage.
Stable isotope probing feeds substrates enriched in 13C, 15N or heavy-oxygen water and traces labelled DNA or RNA to find which taxa are active.

distinct_from: Arbuscular mycorrhizal effects on soil communities

title: Strigolactones

definition.text: Carotenoid-derived signalling molecules that plant roots secrete into the rhizosphere, where they stimulate arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.

facts.text: They make fungal spores in the soil germinate, boost the fungi's metabolism, growth and branching, and prompt the fungi to send signals the plant can detect.
With soil phosphorus they control how fungal hyphae grow through soil; low soil phosphorus increases hyphal branching and the plant's exudation of branching signals.
Hyphae grown in exudates from phosphorus-starved roots grew more and branched further than those in exudates from well-supplied plants.
The parasitic plant Striga also detects strigolactones, germinating and then feeding on the root.
First isolated from cotton roots in 1966, they induce germination of parasitic Striga seeds at trace amounts of about 5 parts per million.
Inside the plant they act as hormones that inhibit shoot branching.
Because Striga depends on them, strigolactone mimics and altered strigolactone blends in maize are proposed ways to fight the parasitic weed.

notes: No Strigolactone article crawled; passes the two-or-more-pages test (Rhizosphere, Arbuscular mycorrhiza, Mycorrhiza, Common symbiosis signaling pathway).

definition.text: A mycorrhiza in which the fungus sheathes the root tip and grows between the root's outer cells without entering them.

facts.text: Its fungi, mostly Basidiomycota and Ascomycota, form a mantle up to 40 μm thick and a Hartig net between epidermal and cortical cells, with hyphae reaching several centimetres into the soil.
It forms on about 2% of plant species, mostly woody plants of families such as birch, beech, willow, pine and rose, but these dominate their ecosystems and much plant biomass.
Nitrogen is scarce in most ecosystems and locked in hard-to-break-down organic matter; the fungi reach further than roots and extract nitrogen from the organic layer.
The fungi are estimated to receive about 15% of the host's food and in return supply up to 86% of its nitrogen needs.
With heavy fertiliser nitrogen plants divert resources from the fungi; in one study species fell from over 30 at low-nitrogen sites to 9 at high-nitrogen sites.
Ectomycorrhizas are usually sampled in surface horizons, where roots are densest, but occur on tree roots at least 4 m deep.
Many European ectomycorrhizal fungi have declined because of poorer tree vitality, forest conversion, pollution and acidification of forest soils.
Laccaria bicolor lures and kills springtails for nitrogen; eastern white pine inoculated with it got up to 25% of its nitrogen from springtails.

verification.title: A strong species–area relationship for eukaryotic soil microbes: island size matters for ectomycorrhizal fungi
verification.evidence: In this study, we examine the species richness of a dominant group of eukaryotic soil microbes, ectomycorrhizal fungi, on 'tree islands' of constant age and host composition that range in size from < 10 to > 10,000 m(2).
verification.note: the paper's 10 m2 is the size of tree islands it sampled; the entry gives the rooting depth of ectomycorrhizas (4 m)

image.caption: Ellen Larsson, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

definition.text: The ability of ectomycorrhizal fungi to survive, and help their hosts survive, soils high in heavy metals, salts, radionuclides and organic pollutants.

facts.text: They limit heavy-metal uptake by sorption at the cell wall and lock metals inside cells in complexes, metallothioneins or vacuoles; they can also concentrate metals in fruiting bodies.
Metal tolerance seems widespread, yet contaminated sites have less diverse fungal communities, while naturally metal-rich serpentine soils do not.
Suillus luteus and S. bovinus have ecotypes adapted to zinc, cadmium and copper.
Some species help hosts survive high soil salinity, some decompose persistent organic pollutants such as PCBs, and many hyperaccumulate radionuclides.

title: Ectomycorrhizae in forestry

definition.text: The use of ectomycorrhizal fungi as inoculum when planting trees and when restoring disturbed ecosystems.

facts.text: Trees transplanted far from home or with specific partners, such as Eucalyptus and Pinus in plantations, often need native ectomycorrhizal inoculum to prosper.
Losing mycorrhizal fungi from a habitat is a major soil disturbance, so adding them back is an important part of restoring vegetation.
Pine and eucalyptus plantations are promoted as carbon sinks, but their ectomycorrhizal fungi tend to deplete soil carbon, which makes this use controversial.
Ectomycorrhizal fungi matter little in farming, since most mycorrhizal crops partner with arbuscular fungi.

contested_note: The source calls planting ectomycorrhizal pine and eucalyptus as carbon sinks controversial, because their fungi tend to deplete soil carbon.

definition.text: A mutualism between plants of the heath family (Ericaceae) and several lineages of mycorrhizal fungi.

facts.text: It adapts heath plants to the acidic, nutrient-poor soils they usually grow in, such as those of boreal forests, bogs and heathlands.
The fungi form coils inside the epidermal cells of fine hair roots; the coils, where soil nutrients are traded for plant sugars, work for only a few weeks before degrading.

The fungi have enzymes that break down complex organic molecules, mainly to reach organic nitrogen where mineral nitrogen is very scarce; they can take nitrogen from cellulose, lignin, pectin and chitin.
In mor humus and OH horizons, ericoid and ectomycorrhizal fungi decompose recalcitrant organic matter and pass its nitrogen straight to their host plants.

title: Glomeromycota

definition.text: A group of fungi, with about 230 described species, whose members form arbuscular mycorrhizas with plant roots.

facts.text: Its arbuscular species live in soils worldwide, partnering the roots of most plant species (over 80%), and also occur in wetlands including salt marshes.
Most evidence shows they depend on land plants for carbon and energy, and this biotrophic habit long hindered growing them in the laboratory.
They reproduce asexually by spores 80–500 μm across; new colonisation depends on the inoculum in the soil, and colonisation rate tracks spore density.
A metatranscriptomic survey of arid land found 5.4% of fungal rRNA reads were Glomeromycota, suggesting earlier PCR-based studies had underestimated their abundance.

conflicts.text: Mycorrhiza says 244 species of Glomeromycota have been identified from spore differences, and genetic studies suggest 300–1600 may exist.
conflicts.note: Against about 230 described species on Glomeromycota.

notes: The page notes the phylum name is now invalid and the subphylum Glomeromycotina should be used (S:b5d22fa5c8ae); kept the article title.

definition.text: Soil bacteria that fix nitrogen once they have settled inside the root nodules of legumes.

facts.text: They need a plant host to fix nitrogen; they live freely in the soil, and when the legume dies its nodules break down and release them back into the soil.
Inside nodules they turn atmospheric N2 into ammonia, which is exported from the nodule and used for the legume's growth.
In this classic mutualism the bacteria supply ammonia or amino acids and receive organic acids, mainly malate and succinate, as their carbon and energy source.
Rhizobium leguminosarum, the first known species, was identified in 1889; rhizobia are a mixed group of alpha- and betaproteobacteria, mostly in the order Hyphomicrobiales.
Much fixed nitrogen leaves with harvested grain or hay, but enough stays in the soil, as higher soil nitrate, to feed the next crop, which matters most where no fertiliser is used.
Inoculation with rhizobia tends to raise yields; 12–20 million hectares of soybeans are inoculated each year, and inoculants have been used in North America for over 100 years.
Cheater strains can hoard plant resources while fixing little nitrogen; legumes answer by sanctioning poorly fixing nodules, cutting their growth or their carbon or oxygen supply.
The mutualism depends on conditions: nutrient deposition has favoured less productive strains, and extra nitrogen lets other plants outcompete legumes for light.

verification.title: Long-term nitrogen addition causes the evolution of less-cooperative mutualists
verification.evidence: Using a long-term (22 years) N-addition experiment, we find that elevated N inputs have altered the legume-rhizobium mutualism (where rhizobial bacteria trade N in exchange for photosynthates from legumes), causing the evolution of less-mutualistic rhizobia.
verification.note: the paper's 22 years is the length of its N-addition experiment; the entry gives how long inoculants have been used (100 years)

definition.text: A growth on the roots of some plants, chiefly legumes, that houses nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

facts.text: Nodules form under nitrogen-poor conditions with host-specific rhizobia in legumes or Frankia in other plants; plenty of soil nitrogen blocks their development.
Legume roots release flavonoids that attract rhizobia and switch on nod factors; these make root hairs curl, and an infection thread carries the bacteria into the cortex.
Fixation is very sensitive to oxygen; leghaemoglobin, an iron-containing protein, manages oxygen supply and turns the fixing zone pink.
The energy to split N2 comes from leaf sugars; malate, a breakdown product of sucrose, feeds the bacteroids directly.
Determinate nodules, as on soybean and bean, stop dividing early and are round; indeterminate ones, as on pea, alfalfa and clover, keep a growing tip and are cylindrical.
Effective nodulation comes about four weeks after planting, and the number and internal colour of nodules show how well nitrogen is being fixed.
Heat, acidic soils, drought and nitrate limit nodulation, and the plant also caps nodule numbers through a signal from its leaves.
When the plant dies its fixed nitrogen is released and fertilises the soil, which is why traditional rotations include a legume such as clover.

image.caption: Nefronus, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

definition.text: A flowering plant that forms a symbiosis with the nitrogen-fixing actinomycete Frankia, which lives in nodules on its roots.

facts.text: They are trees or shrubs, except the herbaceous Datisca, in three orders, eight families and twenty-six genera; alder, bayberry, sea-buckthorn and Casuarina are examples.
Their nodules give them an edge on poor soils, so they pioneer nitrogen-poor ground such as moraines, volcanic flows and sand dunes, enriching the soil for later species.
Some alders fix as much as 300 kg of N2 per hectare per year, close to the highest legume rates, and actinorhizal plants fix roughly as much nitrogen as rhizobial symbioses.
Frankia enters through curled root hairs or between epidermal cells; as in legumes, nitrogen shortage favours nodulation and plentiful nitrogen inhibits it.

conflicts.text: Root nodule says the non-legume Frankia-nodulated plants belong to 25 genera in 8 families.
conflicts.note: Against twenty-six genera in eight families on Actinorhizal plant.

title: Fungal endophyte defense
article: Plant use of endophytic fungi in defense

definition.text: The use by plants of fungi living inside their tissues as an indirect defence against herbivores.

facts.text: In exchange for carbohydrates, the fungi can increase the plant's water or nutrient uptake and protect it from insects, birds or mammals.
Once established, the fungi change the plant's nutrient content and start or boost production of defensive secondary metabolites.
Infection reduces even below-ground herbivores such as nematodes and root-feeding insects.
Fungal toxins in forage harm livestock, causing fescue toxicosis and more than 600 million dollars in livestock deaths each year.

sources.title: Plant use of endophytic fungi in defense
sources.key: Plant use of endophytic fungi in defense

title: Legume family (Fabaceae)

definition.text: The legume or pea family of flowering plants, about 19,000 species, including soybean, beans, pea, chickpea and alfalfa.

facts.text: Many legumes host rhizobia in root nodules, which take nitrogen gas from the air and turn it into a form the plant can use.
Nodule formation is common throughout the family, though rarer in the Caesalpinioideae, and some species in every subfamily do not nodulate.
Rhizobia are host-specific, but one plant can host several kinds: Acacia senegal nodules can hold seven rhizobial species from three genera.
Because of their nodules, legumes are used in crop rotations, and green-manure crops are commonly legumes.

notes: Dossier definition line (S:cc25c45598a4) is a taxonomic fragment, so the definition is built from the lead and Cover crop. S:022ade26ad85 says rhizobia make NO3− or NH3; Rhizobia and Root nodule give ammonia only, so the fact avoids naming the form.

definition.text: A genus of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi whose species all form mycorrhizae with plant roots.

facts.text: With about 85 described species it is the largest genus of arbuscular fungi, though it is not a natural (monophyletic) group.
Its species are thought to be obligate symbionts that cannot be cultured without a host, and they occur in nearly all land habitats, from arable land and deserts to tundra.
Several species, such as G. aggregatum, are cultured and sold as mycorrhizal inoculant for farm soils, while G. macrocarpum causes tobacco stunt disease.

definition.text: An arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus, formerly called Glomus intraradices, used as a soil inoculant in agriculture and horticulture.

facts.text: It occurs in almost all soils, especially in forests and grasslands, and most crops benefit from inoculation with it.
Studies show it increases phosphorus uptake in many plants and improves soil aggregation through its hyphae, which is why it is common in mycorrhizal fertilisers.
It colonises new plants from spores, hyphae or colonised root fragments, and is widely used in research on how arbuscular fungi improve plants and soil.

definition.text: The network of fungal hyphae that grows between the epidermal and cortical cells of a root in an ectomycorrhiza.

facts.text: It is where fungus and plant trade: nutrients gathered from the soil by the outer mycelium are released into the root's apoplast, and plant sugars pass back to feed the fungus.
It supplies the root with nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, micronutrients and water carried through the hyphae.
With Pinaceae hosts it reaches deep into the root cortex, but with many flowering-plant hosts it may not go beyond the epidermis.
It is named after the German forest biologist Theodor Hartig, who reported on this root–fungus interface in 1842.

image.caption: Atrebe10, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

definition.text: The symbiosis between orchids and the endomycorrhizal fungi that colonise their roots and seeds.

facts.text: Orchid seeds, 0.35–1.50 mm long, carry virtually no energy reserve, so seedlings get their carbon from the fungus and nearly all orchids depend on it at some stage.
Inside root cortex cells the fungus forms coils called pelotons, the structure that defines orchid mycorrhiza; the plant can later digest them for carbon and nitrogen.
The fungi are typically basidiomycetes such as Ceratobasidium (Rhizoctonia), Sebacina, Tulasnella and Russula.
Soil phosphorus deficiency often dictates whether the symbiosis forms; the fungus takes phosphorus from organic phosphorus, phosphate and inorganic compounds in the soil.

definition.text: The passive movement of water by plant roots from moist soil to dry soil.

facts.text: It happens in plants rooted in both wet and dry soil, especially those with taproots reaching the water table and lateral roots near the surface.
In drought, groundwater is drawn up the taproot and released from the laterals into the dry surface soil; under flooding, roots move water the other way.
Xylem links from taproot to laterals let wet or dry conditions at the laterals set up a pressure gradient, much like transpirational pull.
Once described as roots releasing water and nutrients into soil mostly at night ('hydraulic lift'), it is now seen as two-way movement helped by mycorrhizal networks.
Hydraulic lift is regulated by the root endodermis and leaf stomata and can be broken by cavitation in the xylem.
Roots doing this smooth out differences in soil moisture, which affects crop irrigation and helps seedlings establish.
It is traced with deuterium, sap flow and soil moisture measurements, and efforts are under way to add it to land-surface models.

definition.text: Soils whose microbes keep pathogens from establishing in the rhizosphere of plants.

facts.text: They develop as plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria settle around roots and outcompete pathogens by releasing suppressive metabolites.
Pathogenic fungi reaching the rhizosphere release enzymes that break down root cell walls; beneficial Pseudomonas and Bacillus make metabolites that break up the fungal hyphae.
Plants under attack recruit these bacteria from the bulk soil through their exudates, but only microbes already in the soil can be recruited.
Greater plant diversity brings greater microbial diversity in the rhizosphere and can mean stronger disease suppression.
Informed crop rotation and soil solarization can create suppressive soils.
Such soils can also make plants more resistant to leaf-feeding insects by promoting beneficial bacteria and priming plant defences.

title: Nitrogen nutrition in the arbuscular mycorrhizal system
article: Nitrogen nutrition in the arbuscular mycorrhizal system

definition.text: The uptake of soil nitrogen by arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and its transfer to host plants and between plants.

facts.text: The extraradical mycelium reaches far into the soil and takes up nitrogen as ammonium, nitrate or organic compounds; the intraradical mycelium inside the root is where the exchange happens.
In vitro, 29% to 50% of root nitrogen has been taken up via the fungus; a 2005 model has it moved as arginine and released to the plant as ammonium.

Nitrogen can move between plants through common mycorrhizal networks: about 25% of labelled nitrogen given to a grass passed to a grapevine, though a soybean–corn field study found negligible transfer.
A growth benefit from fungal nitrogen has not been shown conclusively, some researchers doubt it matters much in nature, and under high nitrogen the fungi can turn parasitic.

contested_note: Research shows arbuscular fungi transfer nitrogen to and between plants, but some researchers doubt they contribute significantly to plant nitrogen in nature.
notes: Dossier definition line (S:8085e7b68bc0) is truncated ('refers to...'); the definition is built from two body sentences.

title: Common symbiosis signaling pathway

definition.text: A highly conserved chain of signals in plant root cells that lets plants take in symbiotic microbes such as arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and rhizobia.

facts.text: It is the ancestral pathway for arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, and the younger root-nodule symbiosis with rhizobia uses it too, so both Myc factors and Nod factors switch it on.
Receptor kinases at the cell membrane perceive the factors; the signal reaches the nucleus as calcium oscillations, decoded by CCaMK, which activates CYCLOPS to start arbuscule or nodule genes.
Its origins predate the colonisation of land by plants, showing that plants and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi have co-evolved for over 500 million years.
Rhizobia probably co-opted the older endomycorrhizal signalling, since the two processes share genes such as the receptor SYMRK.

notes: Frame candidate for this chapter; crawled but not in the dossier.

definition.text: Cluster roots, also called proteoid roots, are roots that form clusters of closely spaced short lateral rootlets.

facts.text: They may form a mat 2 to 5 cm thick beneath the leaf litter and appear under low phosphate or low iron, enhancing nutrient uptake, possibly by chemically modifying the soil to dissolve nutrients.
They let plants grow in very nutrient-poor soils, such as the phosphorus-deficient native soils of Australia.
Adolf Engler first described them in 1894 on Proteaceae; they are now known in 27 Proteaceae genera and about 30 species of other families, and in crops such as lupins and macadamia.
Cultivated plants with cluster roots need slow-release, low-phosphorus fertilizers, since higher levels cause phosphorus toxicity and sometimes iron deficiency.

definition.text: Small iron-binding compounds secreted by microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi, and by some plants, to gather iron.

facts.text: In aerobic soils iron is mostly ferric (Fe3+), which forms insoluble rust-like solids; siderophores pull it into soluble complexes that cells take up by active transport.
They are among the strongest known Fe3+ binders, and microbes switch on their production when iron runs short.
Plant iron deficiency is a problem on calcareous soils, 30% of the world's farmland; grasses, cereals and rice respond by secreting phytosiderophores such as deoxymugineic acid into the rhizosphere.

Soil Actinomycetales, Bacillus, Arthrobacter and Nocardia secrete ferrioxamines that also feed other microbes; fungi such as Aspergillus and Penicillium make ferrichromes that resist breakdown in humic soil.
In decaying litter with pH as low as 3–4, organisms making acid-stable hydroxamate siderophores have an advantage.
Siderophores made by rhizosphere microbes raise iron availability to plants; oats, for example, can take up iron through them.
Fluorescent pseudomonads, biocontrol agents against some soil-borne pathogens, make pyoverdine siderophores that deprive pathogens of iron.
Siderophores can also chelate other metals, including aluminium, copper, zinc, lead, manganese, cadmium and uranium.

definition.text: The zone of soil, rich in microbes, around the underground parts of plant stems; it is the stem's counterpart of the rhizosphere and spermosphere.

facts.text: The name comes from the Greek laimos ('throat'), for a connecting neck, plus -sphere for a zone of influence.
It surrounds any underground plant organ other than roots, such as hypocotyls, stems, stolons, corms, bulbs and leaves, where exuded sugars and amino acids stimulate microbes.
As a seedling grows, the spermosphere extends downward into the rhizosphere and upward into the laimosphere around the stem.
Exudates there can wake pathogens such as Fusarium, Phytophthora, Pythium and Rhizoctonia, which start the hypocotyl and stem rots of damping-off.

definition.text: The small organ, also called the calyptra, that covers the tip of every growing plant root.

facts.text: It shields the root's apical meristem from damage, lubricates its passage through soil and houses gravity-sensing cells that steer its growth.
Statoliths settling in its statocytes drive gravitropism; if the cap is removed, the root grows at random.
It secretes a mucilage layer that reduces friction and may foster signalling with soil microbes.
It is renewed continuously as the oldest outer layers slough off, in cereals and many legumes as long-lived border cells.

definition.text: Specialized aerial roots that let plants breathe air where the soil is waterlogged.

facts.text: They grow down from the stem or up from ordinary roots; some botanists call them aerating roots when they emerge from the soil.
Porous lenticels lead into air-filled aerenchyma, which helps gases spread through the plant, since oxygen diffuses four orders of magnitude faster in air than in water.
Black and grey mangroves bear them, and mangrove aerial roots serve aeration rather than water uptake.
Cypress knees were thought to be pneumatophores, but they lack aerenchyma and exchange little gas, and their function remains unclear.

definition.text: A genus of filamentous nitrogen-fixing bacteria that live in root nodules of actinorhizal plants, much as rhizobia do in legumes.

facts.text: With the enzyme nitrogenase they turn atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia and can meet most or all of the host's nitrogen needs, so hosts thrive in nutrient-poor soils.
Most strains are specific to particular hosts, which include all alders, some Casuarina species, sea-buckthorn and its relatives, Myrica and Ceanothus.
They infect through deformed root hairs or between root cells; either way a nodule primordium forms, fed through the plant's vascular tissue.
Brunchorst named the genus in 1886, taking it for a fungus; Becking redefined it in 1970 as a prokaryotic actinomycete.

definition.text: Signalling molecules that rhizobia release in response to legume flavonoids and that trigger the formation of root nodules.

facts.text: They are lipochitooligosaccharides: chains of N-acetyl-D-glucosamine carrying a fatty acid, with strain-specific substitutions.
Flavonoids from the plant activate the bacterial regulator NodD, which switches on the nod genes that make them.
LysM receptor kinases, NFR1 and NFR5, first isolated in Lotus japonicus in 2003, perceive them; calcium influx then depolarizes root-hair membranes and starts early nodulin genes.
The root hair curls round the bacteria and an infection thread carries them to inner cortex cells, which become the nodule primordium where they fix nitrogen as bacteroids.

definition.text: A microbe, often a bacterium or fungus, that lives inside a plant for at least part of its life without causing apparent disease.

facts.text: Endophytes have been found in every plant species studied so far, yet most of these relationships are poorly understood.
They pass from parent to offspring through seeds (vertical transmission) or spread between plants by spores (horizontal transmission).
Often mutualists, they help hosts cope with pathogens, drought, heat, poor soils, salinity and herbivory, and receive carbon in return.
Systemic endophytes stay harmless for the plant's whole life, while non-systemic ones vary with conditions and can turn pathogenic when the host is stressed.
They can raise uptake of soil-limited nutrients such as phosphorus and make rock phosphate and atmospheric nitrogen available to the plant.
Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi are one group of fungal endophytes; bacterial endophytes come from many unrelated taxa.
Fungicides harm endophytic fungi and fertilizers lessen a plant's reliance on them; Epichloë endophytes are used commercially in turf grasses.

title: Azospirillum

definition.text: A genus of Gram-negative, microaerophilic nitrogen-fixing bacteria that can promote plant growth.

facts.text: They live in soil and fresh water, especially in close association with roots; over 113 plant species in 35 families have benefited from them.
Many excrete plant hormones that make roots grow more branches and fine root hairs, and they make nitrogen and phosphorus more available to plants.
They also curb disease by competing with pathogens for space and iron and by priming induced systemic resistance; how much nitrogen they supply by fixation is debated.
Johanna Döbereiner's group in Brazil found root-associated strains that fix nitrogen in the 1970s; commercial inoculants appeared in 2009 and exceeded 3 million doses a year by 2018.

contested_note: The source says how much nitrogen Azospirillum contributes to crops through biological fixation is debated.

definition.text: A genus of Gram-negative soil bacteria, many of which fix nitrogen in the root nodules of legumes.

facts.text: They are slow-growing rhizobia, taking 3–5 days to cloud a liquid medium, unlike the fast-growing Rhizobium.
Bradyrhizobium japonicum nodulates soybeans, cowpeas and mung beans, and commercial inoculants are available.
They are also major members of forest soil microbial communities, where strains usually cannot fix nitrogen or form nodules.
Grain legumes grown on about 1.5 million km2 a year fix about 44–66 million tons of nitrogen, almost half of the nitrogen used in agriculture.

definition.text: A genus of aerobic, rod-shaped, nitrogen-fixing soil bacteria that live in the root nodules of mainly legumes.

facts.text: In nodules they convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia with nitrogenase and pass it to the plant as glutamine or ureides, receiving photosynthate in return.
Martinus Beijerinck first isolated a microbe from legume nodules in 1888, naming it Bacillus radicicola; it is now placed in Rhizobium.
Rhizobium can also solubilise phosphate.
Rhizobium rhizogenes is a pathogen that causes hairy root disease by injecting root-inducing T-DNA into plants.

definition.text: The mass of fungal hyphae growing out into the soil from ectomycorrhizas, also called extraradical mycelium.

facts.text: It may be fine, frequently branching hyphae that explore the soil or aggregate into rhizomorphs, durable water-repellent transport structures that work like xylem.
It is the fungus's main body: the site of mineral uptake and enzyme production, a way to colonise new root tips, and food for invertebrates.
Because ectomycorrhizas are small, the extra hyphae greatly enlarge the surface in contact with soil, reaching water and nutrients roots cannot.
Lab studies predict about 23% of plant carbon goes to it, 15-30% of that lost to respiration; it may hold a third of microbial biomass and half the dissolved organic carbon in some forest soils.
Its hyphae excrete compounds into soil that account for as much as 40% of their total carbon use.
It is where phosphorus is gathered, and starving the host plant of phosphorus can increase its growth tenfold.
It proliferates more in mineral soil than in organic material and may be absent from fresh leaf litter.
Its lifespan, from a few months to several years, is estimated with ergosterol or PLFA analysis, 14C dating or sand-filled ingrowth bags.

definition.text: A classification of ectomycorrhizal fungi by the growth pattern and biomass of their extramatrical mycelium and whether they form rhizomorphs.

facts.text: Agerer proposed exploration types in 2001; four are commonly recognised: contact, short-distance, medium-distance and long-distance.
Long-distance types form rhizomorphs with hollow, vessel-like tubes, take up more organic nitrogen and are thought less competitive in disturbed systems.
In pine systems long-distance types dominate where roots are sparse and short-distance types where roots are dense, being cheaper in carbon.
Many fungi fall along a gradient rather than into one type; exploration types of over 550 species are compiled in the DEEMY database.

definition.text: A plant root usually defined as two millimetres or less in diameter.

facts.text: Fine roots take up soil resources such as water and nutrients and/or transport them, making them the root-system counterpart of leaves and twigs.
They make up most of a root system's length and respond to nutrient patches by lengthening, branching more and starting more lateral roots.
Fine-root biomass and nitrogen concentration decrease with soil depth.
Their formation, death and decomposition can account for 20-80% of net primary production in forest carbon and nutrient cycles.
They release labile carbon in exudates, feeding soil organic carbon directly and by stimulating microbes.
Root tensile strength rises as diameter falls, so fine roots are stronger than coarse roots and help reinforce slopes against erosion.
In trees, fine roots are usually colonised by a single mycorrhizal type, arbuscular or ecto.

definition.text: Schemes that divide fine roots by diameter, position in the branching hierarchy or function.

facts.text: The traditional two-millimetre cutoff is arbitrary; roots under 0.5 mm are called very fine roots.
Order-based classes follow the Horton–Strahler scheme: unbranched distal tips are first-order, and two roots of the same order join to form the next order.
Diameter, life span and secondary growth increase with root order, while nitrogen content, mycorrhizal colonization and turnover decrease.
Function-based classes separate absorptive fine roots, the low-order distal segments, from transport fine roots formed where they merge.

verification.title: Very fine roots respond to soil depth: biomass allocation, morphology, and physiology in a broad‐leaved temperate forest
verification.evidence: Abstract Very fine roots (<0.5 mm in diameter) of forest trees may serve as better indicators of root function than the traditional category of <2 mm, but how these roots will exhibit the plasticity of species‐specific traits in response to heterogeneous soil nutrients is unknown.

verification.title: Redefining fine roots improves understanding of below‐ground contributions to terrestrial biosphere processes
verification.evidence: Traditionally, fine roots have been defined as all roots ≤ 2 mm in diameter, yet it is now recognized that this approach fails to capture the diversity of form and function observed among fine‐root orders.

definition.text: A root that grows out sideways from the primary root, arising in the pericycle, and builds up the branching pattern of a root system.

facts.text: Lateral roots anchor the plant, increase water uptake and nutrient extraction, and enlarge the root system's surface area.
Some form symbioses with rhizobia and mycorrhizal fungi that further raise nutrient uptake.
Their number matches the number of xylem bundles, and two lateral roots never form directly opposite each other.
The hormone auxin (IAA) is required at several stages of their development.

definition.text: Signal molecules produced within plants in extremely low concentrations that control growth and development.

facts.text: Every plant cell can make hormones, and they are not nutrients but chemicals that in small amounts steer cell growth and differentiation.
Fungi and bacteria make very similar chemicals that also affect plant growth, though in microbes they act as secondary metabolites.
Auxins promote root initiation and lateral and adventitious root growth; synthetic auxins such as IBA and NAA are sold as rooting powders for cuttings.
When roots run short of water a signal triggers ABA formation; roots release ABA to the leaves, where it closes the stomata.
When a growing root hits an obstacle underground, ethylene production surges and halts cell elongation.
Strigolactones exuded into soil promote the growth of symbiotic arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.
Went and Thimann coined the term phytohormone in their 1937 book.

definition.text: Soil bacteria that associate with ectomycorrhizal and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and improve the symbiosis.

facts.text: They come from many phyla; Pseudomonas and Streptomyces are the most commonly reported, and Bacillus is another.
They enhance mycorrhizal growth and function and nutrient uptake by fungus and plant, help against some pathogens and promote defences.
Some weather minerals, releasing protons and iron that lower soil pH and recycle nutrients.
Phosphate-solubilising rhizobacteria build a phosphate pool that mycorrhizas use, helping them establish where phosphorus is limiting.
Some fix nitrogen in the soil around mycorrhizas, without the root modifications legumes make.
In soils rich in toxic metals they help block plant uptake of lead, zinc and cadmium, making them candidates for bioremediation.
Most studies show them fighting pathogens with acids and antifungal metabolites, but in a few cases they aided pathogenic fungi.
How these interactions work is not well understood.

definition.text: The zone made up of roots, the hyphae of their mycorrhizal fungi, associated microorganisms and the soil under their direct influence.

facts.text: Here roots release nutrients and the fungus raises microbial numbers and activity.
Hyphae are thinner than roots and reach moisture and nutrients that roots cannot.
Mycorrhizal fungi can ward off pathogens: Glomus intraradices reduces germination of Fusarium oxysporum but stimulates the harmless Trichoderma harzianum.
Its bacteria affect nutrient uptake, protect against pathogens and contribute to nitrogen fixation and mineral weathering.
The mycorrhiza type shapes protozoan numbers: a Paxillus involutus mycorrhiza lowers protozoan density, whereas Lactarius rufus and Suillus bovinus raise it.
Nematodes, mites and earthworms forage on its roots, hyphae and microbes.

definition.text: The ways the timing, machinery and chemicals of farming help or harm the mycorrhizosphere that crops rely on for nutrients and pathogen resistance.

facts.text: Intercropping and reduced tillage, herbicide and fertiliser use increase arbuscular mycorrhizal colonization.
Hyphae secrete adhesive glomalin that builds stable aggregates and resists erosion, accounting for about 5% of global organic carbon and nitrogen storage.
Monocropping, frequent tillage that severs hyphal networks, and fertilisers that reduce plant reliance on the fungi all weaken the symbiosis.
Mesoamerican milpa farming limits tillage and fertiliser; maize intercropped with beans yields more through the shared mycorrhizosphere.

definition.text: Non-pathogenic, filamentous soil fungi that colonise roots, chiefly in the rhizosphere, and benefit plant health and development.

facts.text: They are the fungal counterpart of PGPR; mycorrhizal fungi are not counted among them, and most belong to the Ascomycota.
Directly, they make auxins such as IAA that shape root architecture, solubilise phosphorus with organic acids and capture iron with siderophores.
Indirectly, they suppress harmful soil microbes through antibiotics, mycoparasitism and competition, and trigger induced systemic resistance.
Some Trichoderma species can remediate heavy metals, organometallic compounds and agrochemicals.

definition.text: A process in which plants change the biological and physical qualities of their soil, which then changes how well plants can grow in it later.

facts.text: Feedback is negative when a species grows worse in soil previously occupied by its own kind, and positive when it grows better.
Negative feedback was once blamed on nutrient depletion; recent work points mainly to a build-up of soil-borne pathogens, with mutualists and allelopathy also involved.
On average feedback tends to be negative, with many exceptions such as many invasive species.
Negative feedback helps species coexist: abundant plants accumulate their pathogens, while rare plants escape them.
Negative plant–soil feedback has been called a particular case of the Janzen–Connell hypothesis.

It is best measured with Bever's interaction coefficient, Is = Gx(home) + Gy(home) − Gx(away) − Gy(away), from growth of two species in own- and other-conditioned soil; a negative Is favours coexistence.

definition.text: An ecological interaction between two or more species in which each gains a net benefit.

facts.text: About 80% of land plant species rely on mycorrhizal fungi for inorganic compounds and trace elements, a 'biological barter' of plant carbohydrates for minerals.
Rhizobia fix nitrogen for legumes in return for carbohydrates; in Three Sisters farming, beans fix nitrogen in the soil for the corn they climb.
Mutualism with mycorrhizal fungi is linked to the colonisation of land by plants.
Plant lineages in nutrient-rich environments have abandoned mycorrhizal mutualism many times, and mutualistic fungi can turn parasitic on weak or dying plants.

definition.text: An underground laboratory built to study soil and its interactions with plants and animals.

facts.text: A central corridor usually has viewing windows into the soil profiles on either side.
Separate outside bays allow experiments that vary the soil composition and the plants and animals in it.
Rhizotrons operate at Kew Gardens, a USDA research station in Houghton, Michigan, Treborth Botanic Garden in Wales and Charles Sturt University in Australia.

definition.text: A Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium closely related to K. pneumoniae and distinguished from it by indole production.

facts.text: It is a diazotroph that colonises plant hosts and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can use.
It has been shown to associate with the barley rhizosphere through an entire vegetative period.
The bacteria adhere strongly to root hairs and less strongly to the elongation zone and root cap mucilage.
